title: First recordings and the 1930s repertoire
summary: He recalls early Brunswick, Vocalion and Victor sessions and tunes like 'Uproar Shout' and 'Swinging in Harlem'.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Now, when did you begin recording the band? You mentioned the recording session.
Brunswick. "Dear Old Southland", I believe, in a session for them in 1936. I don't remember other tunes. "Weary", no "Weary Blues" we did for Victor.
And then, we did something for Vocalion, I believe.
Right. "Uproar Shout" and things like that.
Yeah. That's it. I forgot about that.
Yeah. And then I think, not too long after that we went with [RCA]Victor when I think was, must have been '37 or '38.
How would you explain the style that you were using around the time that you were doing "Uproar Shout" and things like that?

Well, we stayed with almost, it's a Swing style. But, "Uproar Shout", I'm trying to figure out who made that arrangement. I don't know if it was Bill Johnson or even Sam Lowe. I don't remember just who. But, we stayed with that tempo. That tempo was the
one that I liked, you know. But, I took the arrangement. I couldn't, I don't remember just who made it. But, it was a good feeling that we had, and the solo was part we built on.
I think "Swinging in Harlem" was during that era too. We did it. You know "Swinging in Harlem"?

The same with "Coquette". All those tunes were somewhere near the same beat, same tempo I should say. "Swing a Little Rhythm". Some of these names I haven't seen in a long time. I forgot the meaning. "Way Down Upon The Swanee River". (Inaudible). All, yeah, most of this was with RCA Victor, right?
"I'll See You In My Dreams", "Red Cap", "I Found A New Baby", "Carry Me Back To Ole Virginny", "Let Me Dream".
Now, some of these tunes got to come back to me.
